newsitem.title: JAPAN: FREESTYLE SKIING-ACRO STILL SEEKING OLYMPIC RESPECT.
newsitem.headline: FREESTYLE SKIING-ACRO STILL SEEKING OLYMPIC RESPECT.

text.p: Fabrice Becker of France won the men's acro event at the world freestyle skiing championships on Friday, then said the discipline was in danger of disappearing unless a decision about its Olympic status was made soon.
The self-coached Becker led the 19-man field with 26.90 points despite a neck injury which kept him from competing in aerials qualifications earlier in the week.
American Don Edmondson was second in the acro -- previously known as ballet -- with 26.40 points while Heini Baumgartner of Switzerland scored 25.40 to place third.
Oksana Kushenko of Russia, skiing in a cossack-inspired costume to the strains of a Russian folk song, won the women's event with 25.80 points.
Swedes took the next two spots with identical scores of 25.25 but Asa Magnussons higher technical mark earned her second place ahead of Annika Johansson.
Becker, the only French acro competitor in Nagano, said he was self-coached because the French ski federation was reluctant to fund coaching for a non-Olympic sport.

French national champinnships are no longer held in acro for lack of competitors, said Bernard Manuel, International Ski Federation (FIS) technical delegate, who called Becker "the last of a generation".
"A decision about acro needs to be made soon," said Becker. "Before the 2002 Olympics."
Edmondson echoed Becker's remarks, saying he hoped acro's exclusion would end with the 2002 Winter Olympics in Salt Lake City.
"This kind of musicality and artistry belong out there," said Edmondson.
"It's not just sports with clocks that should be in the Olympics," said Baumgartner, World Cup acro champion.
Olympic officials admitted moguls for the 1992 Albertville Games and aerials two years later at Lillehammer.
But their decision to ignore acro has left the discipline as the sport's poor relation, with many veterans forsaking it to specialise in moguls or aerials and fewer young skiers taking it up.

The men's and women's events at Mount Iizuna, which will host mogul and aerial competitions at next year's Nagano Olympics, each drew less than 20 entries. In comparison, the men's moguls attracted more than 40 entrants.
CBS, the American television network, which paid $375 million for U.S. rights to the Nagano Games, is covering moguls and aerials at the world championships but not acro.
In a bid to emphasise the sport's athleticism, the FIS changed the discipline's name from ballet to acro in 1995.
